Summary: Voluntary, sector-agnostic framework (Identify, Measure, Manage, Govern) to help organizations manage AI risks across the lifecycle. Includes core functions, categories, and informative references; supported by an online Playbook, Profiles, and crosswalks to other standards.
Healthcare Implications: Hospitals, payers, and vendors can use the RMF to structure governance for clinical and operational AI – e.g., risk registers, impact assessments, model cards, and continuous monitoring. Aligns well with health‑specific guidance (e.g., HTI‑1 DSI transparency) and can be profiled for care settings.

Standard Name/Number: Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Nursing Practice
Summary: Sets ethical expectations for AI in nursing: preserve human relationships, ensure safety/competence, maintain privacy, and address bias. Calls for nursing involvement in design, deployment, and evaluation of AI systems impacting practice.
Healthcare Implications: Guides hospital nursing leadership on acceptable AI uses (e.g., ambient documentation, staffing tools), emphasizing training, transparency, and reporting mechanisms for harms or malfunctions.

Standard Name/Number: IEEE 2801-2022 – Recommended Practice for the Quality Management of Datasets for Medical Artificial Intelligence
Summary: Establishes recommended quality-management activities for datasets used in AI-enabled medical devices, including quality objectives and controls for data collection, annotation, transfer, use, storage, maintenance, updating, retirement, records, responsibilities, resources, and quality control.
Healthcare Implications: Medical-AI developers and healthcare data partners can use the standard to structure dataset governance across the lifecycle, document responsibilities and records, and reduce safety and performance failures caused by poorly controlled training, validation, or testing data.

Standard Name/Number: IEEE 7002-2022 – Data Privacy Process
Summary: Specifies a systems/software engineering process for privacy-by-design, including requirements elicitation, data minimization, consent, and lifecycle controls. Applies to products and services processing personal data, including AI systems.
Healthcare Implications: Useful for digital health apps, remote monitoring platforms, and clinical AI tools processing PHI/PII. Supports privacy impact assessments and engineering controls aligned to healthcare compliance expectations.
Keyword Tags: Privacy & Data; Transparency & Governance

Standard Name/Number: NIST SP 1270 – Identifying and Managing Bias in AI
Summary: Provides a structured approach to identifying and managing bias in AI systems, spanning data, human, and systemic sources. Addresses terminology, measurement, and evaluation practices to mitigate harmful outcomes.
Healthcare Implications: Directly applicable to clinical algorithm development and validation (e.g., subgroup performance, fairness metrics). Helps health systems design bias controls and documentation for oversight bodies and quality governance.

Standard Name/Number: IEEE 7001-2021 – Transparency of Autonomous Systems
Summary: Defines requirements for achieving and documenting transparency in autonomous/intelligent systems, including traceability, explainability, and communication to stakeholders. Supports accountability and human oversight by clarifying what information should be available and when.
Healthcare Implications: Applicable to AI-enabled clinical tools (e.g., imaging triage, decision support) to structure explainability artifacts and user communications. Helps providers evaluate vendor claims and set expectations for documentation and post‑market updates.

Summary: Establishes core requirements and a baseline for trustworthy healthcare AI, addressing trust from the perspectives of clinicians, patients, caregivers, public-health organizations, medical societies, and regulators.
Healthcare Implications: Provides healthcare organizations and developers with a sector-specific baseline for assessing governance, transparency, data quality, human oversight, safety, privacy, bias, and regulatory considerations.

Standard Name/Number: CTA-2136 – Operations and Monitoring of Predictive Health AI Solutions
Summary: Provides a risk-based approach to monitoring the accuracy and performance of predictive health AI after deployment, including model drift and transparency about performance and updates. It does not cover generative AI, AI scribes, or initial model training, and does not specify metric thresholds that trigger retraining.
Healthcare Implications: Developers and deploying healthcare organizations can use the standard to structure ongoing performance monitoring and review model changes. It complements the existing CTA-2135 row, which addresses verification and validation before deployment. Adoption is voluntary.

Standard Name/Number: CHI Health AI Roles & Interdependency Framework
Summary: Maps responsibilities across foundation-model and application developers, healthcare organizations, clinicians, payers, patients, and assurance bodies. Its role-specific recommendations address disclosure of intended uses and limitations, clinical validation, organizational oversight, clinician review, patient communication, and the ability to override automated coverage decisions.
Healthcare Implications: Healthcare organizations and vendors can use the framework to identify who should supply evidence, manage risks, oversee use, and communicate limitations at each stage of an AI tool's deployment. Its allocation of responsibilities adds detail beyond general AI governance principles, but creates no binding requirements.

Issuing Body: Spring Health and AI in Mental Health Safety & Ethics Council
Standard Name/Number: VERA-MH v1.2.0 – Validation of Ethical and Responsible AI in Mental Health
Summary: Provides an open-source method for simulating mental health chatbot conversations and scoring responses against a clinician-informed rubric. Its five dimensions assess detection and confirmation of potential risk, guidance toward human care, supportive communication, and appropriate AI boundaries. Version 1.2 revised the rubric with clinician and lived-experience input.
Healthcare Implications: Developers, providers, and purchasers can use the versioned rubric to investigate chatbot responses to sensitive mental health scenarios and compare evaluations run with the same rubric and personas. It supplies a more specific testing method than HAPI's existing general chatbot guidance. A benchmark score is not certification or proof of safety in clinical use.
